problem_evidence.fact: FDA observed 397 retail deli departments in 2015-2016: 70.0% were out of compliance on 'foods requiring refrigeration are held at proper temperature' (data item 5), 62.9% on 'foods are cooled properly' (data item 7), and the improper holding/time-and-temperature risk factor as a whole was out of compliance in 91.2% of delis.

FDA's 10-year trend study (roughly 850 establishments observed per data-collection phase across nine facility types) found that in 2008 only 45% of full-service restaurants and 49% of delis were 'in compliance' with the improper holding (time and temperature) risk factor - i.e. a majority were not.

New Jersey defines 'refrigeration temperatures' as 41 F or less (a 45 F allowance applied only to equipment in use before Jan 2, 2007 that had to be upgraded or replaced by Jan 2, 2012), and requires potentially hazardous food to be held at refrigeration temperatures except during prep/cooking/cooling or approved time-as-control.

NJ's cooling rule is two-stage and the stages are cumulative, not concurrent: N.J.A.C. 8:24-3.5(d)1 reads 'i. Within two hours, from 135 degrees Fahrenheit to 70 degrees Fahrenheit; and ii. Within four hours, from 70 degrees Fahrenheit to refrigeration temperatures.' The four-hour clock starts at 70 F, so the total allowed window is up to six hours, not four - a rule that can only be evidenced with timestamped readings.

avenues.established_pattern: Three independent signals per refrigerated unit, not one: (1) product-simulating temperature probe (probe in a glycol bottle or a buffered simulant, not just air temperature, because air temp swings on every door open and every defrost cycle), (2) magnetic reed/door contact to catch a door left ajar and to suppress nuisance alarms during stocking, (3) power/compressor state from a current clamp or a gateway on a UPS, so a power loss is reported even when the sensor itself is dead. The U.S. DOE Federal Energy Management Program O&M Best Practices Guide (Release 3.0, 2010) states that past studies estimate a properly functioning predictive maintenance program provides 8-12% savings over preventive maintenance alone, and lists industrial-average savings of 35-45% reduction in downtime, 70-75% elimination of breakdowns and 25-30% reduction in maintenance costs. The guide attributes these to unnamed 'independent surveys' with no study, sample size or method given, so treat them as a 2010 vintage aggregate rather than a measured result.

MaintainX's 2024 vendor-run survey of 1,165 maintenance, repair and operations professionals reports the average hour of unplanned downtime at about $25,000, with 29% naming aging equipment as the leading expected cause of unplanned downtime in the next 12 months and 60% citing skilled-trade shortage as the top barrier to improving maintenance. This is self-reported vendor survey data; the press release shows no survey methodology.

A Parts Town survey of approximately 1,800 professionals at chain and institutional organizations, fielded in 2025, reports that one in three respondents experience unplanned equipment downtime every week, and that refrigeration equipment and fryers were identified as both the most frequently failing and the most disruptive equipment. Chain respondents included restaurants, grocery and convenience stores; institutional respondents covered education, healthcare, hospitality and corporate facilities - so this is not a foodservice-only sample. The results were published on Parts Town Unlimited's blog on June 30, 2026 under the title 'New Research Highlights the Real Impact of Equipment Downtime'; the blog does not use the title 'Rethinking Downtime'.

avenues.established_pattern: Two-stage, cheapest-first: (1) hardware-decode camera substreams and use motion/small-model gating to cut frame volume; (2) run a detector (YOLO26/YOLO11 or RF-DETR) on an accelerator at 2-10 fps per camera, track objects (ByteTrack-style) and apply zone/line/dwell rules - this catches the great majority of candidate events at single-digit to low-tens of milliseconds per frame; (3) only when a rule fires, send 1-8 frames or a thumbnail to a small vision-language model to describe and classify the exception in plain language and reject lookalikes; (4) route the result to a human confirmation step (dashboard, SMS, Home Assistant) and write an audit record. Never let step 3 accuse anyone. This is exactly the split Frigate documents: detector and tracker identify and track, VLM describes images collected during the track.
avenues.fine_tuning_needed: Almost never for the VLM, usually yes for the detector. Prompt-and-schema work plus zone rules gets a 3B VLM to a usable description/verdict on day one; LoRA is only worth it when you need rigid JSON output, a house vocabulary ('gloves', 'hairnet', 'dock door'), or consistency across sites. For the detector, the COCO class set does not contain what clients care about (hairnet, glove, pallet jack, spill), so you either pick a class set someone already trained or fine-tune. N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9 makes it a third-degree crime to record another person's intimate parts, or fourth-degree for undergarment-clad intimate parts, where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed; observing a fitting-room access way/foyer is only lawful with conspicuous posted notice at the entrance (subsection e), and subsection f makes it a violation of subsection a. or b. to observe or record a person in a private dressing stall.
